Content: At its core, algebra is the language of patterns, relationships, and problem-solving. While arithmetic allows us to calculate specific numbers, algebra gives us a framework to describe how different quantities interact with each other — letting us solve for unknowns and make predictions about the future. For example, algebra provides the tools to help a business forecast how many products it needs to be profitable or a scientist to model the trajectory of a rocket.

Everyday life is full of changing inputs and outputs. Algebra empowers us to see the underlying structure of these situations — from interest rates to cell phone data plans to travel times to fitness goals. Instead of guessing or doing a new calculation every time a condition changes, algebra allows builds a single mathematical model that can handle any scenario we throw at it. On the SAT, mastering this language can be very helpful for turning complicated word problems into simple and solvable equations.

To understand algebra, we must first master its three fundamental building blocks: constants, variables, and expressions. `ultext(Constants)` are fixed values, like a flat registration fee, that never change regardless of the circumstances. `ultext(Variables)` can take on many possible values, like the number of months during a gym membership, and are usually represented by letters like `x` or `y` as placeholders for numbers that are either unknown or free to change. These components fit together to form `ultext(Expressions)`, which are the meaningful phrases of algebra. Constants and variables are combined with mathematical operations — like addition or multiplication — to create a complete descriptions of real-world scenarios.

In the instance of a gym membership that charges a `$50` fee then `$25` each month, constants and variable combine to form an expression — `25m+50` — for the total cost. In this expression, the constant (`50`) describes the initial cost, the variable (`m`) represents a changing input for the duration of the membership, and the coefficient (`25`) describe the rate of change per month. Together, these building blocks let us calculate the total cost whether we stay at the gym for two months or two years.

When working through complex word problems, we can follow a simple three-step process to construct the correct expression for any scenario. First, identify the constant which represents an initial value or an added amount that never changes. Second, identify the variable which can take on many different values depending on the situation — along with the repeating rate that it might be multiplied with. Third, combine the constant and variable (along with its rate) to create a whole expression. We can even plug in multiple values for the variable to check if the expression makes sense.
